title: Canonical URLs for a studio site
metaTitle: Canonical URLs for a studio site
excerpt: Pick one official URL for each page. Make parameters, trailing slashes, and www agree, or a small site splits into smaller pieces.

faqs.question: What is a canonical URL?
faqs.answer: It is the one official address for a page. Other versions, with a tracking parameter, a trailing slash, or a www host, should agree that this address is the real one. If they do not, a small site gets indexed as several thinner copies of itself.

faqs.question: Should www and the bare host both work?
faqs.answer: Visitors can type either one, and you should send them to a single host. Pick the version you will print, share, and measure, and redirect the other with a permanent redirect. Leaving both as equal addresses splits links and analytics for no benefit.

faqs.question: Do tracking parameters need their own canonical?
faqs.answer: The campaign link can keep its parameter so you can see where the visit came from. The canonical should still point at the clean page, without the parameter. Otherwise every newsletter and every ad starts a new URL that looks like a separate article.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A canonical URL explained without the spec language is the one official address for a page. Every other version should admit that. Parameters, trailing slashes, and www versus the bare host have to agree, or a small studio site splits into smaller pieces.

You do not need a large information architecture to have this problem. Ten pages, each reachable three ways, behave like thirty pages that barely point at each other.

## One address is the page

Pick the URL you would print on a card. That is the official page. It is the one you link to from the navigation, the one you paste into a proposal, and the one you want a search result to show. The others may still resolve, because people type oddly and old links linger. They should not compete.

This is easy to postpone because the site still "works." A founder can open the www version and the bare host and see the same pixels. The damage is quieter than a broken layout. Links land in different buckets. Analytics splits. A person who bookmarked one version and was sent the other cannot tell if they are in the right place. On a site with a handful of essays and a handful of project pages, you cannot afford to cut each one into thirds.

Write the choice down. Host, protocol, trailing slash, and case. Then make the build obey it. A decision that lives only in someone's head will be re-decided by the next redirect, the next campaign tool, and the next preview deploy.

## What "canonical" is asking the crawler

The canonical is a hint: this URL is the one to keep. You send it with a link element in the page, and you should also make the rest of the site behave as if you meant it. Redirect the duplicates you control. Use the official URL in your own navigation, your sitemap, and your internal links. A hint that contradicts your own links is not a hint. It is a shrug.

[Google's title-link guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) is a useful picture of the cost. Google builds the title of a result from the title element, the visible heading, other prominent text, and the anchor text of links that point at the page. If the same essay is available at three addresses, those signals scatter. One version collects the navigation link. Another collects a social share. A third collects an old campaign. None of them looks like the page you thought you published. Google may also rewrite a title that is duplicate, boilerplate, or out of date. Duplicate URLs make that rewrite more likely, because the system is looking at several weak copies instead of one clear page.

You will not see this on day one. Recrawling takes time. The week after launch is the wrong week to judge whether the host choice "does not matter."

## Trailing slashes, www, and parameters

Three mismatches cause almost all of the splits on a studio site.

Trailing slash. Pick one. `/work` or `/work/`. Redirect the other. Do not let the framework emit both in different components. A relative link that sometimes adds the slash will mint duplicates forever. Check the sitemap and the navigation against the same rule. If the sitemap has the slash and the menu does not, you have already voted twice.

Host. Choose www or the bare domain, and redirect the rest to it. HTTPS only. An http version that still returns the page is another copy, and it teaches browsers and people to keep using the insecure one. The certificate should cover the host you chose and the one you redirect, so the redirect itself does not scare anyone with a warning.

Parameters. A tracking parameter is not a new page. `?utm_source=newsletter` should canonicalize back to the clean URL. So should `?ref=twitter`, a stray `?preview=true` that escaped staging, and a filter that does not change the content. If a parameter does change the content, say so honestly, and give that view its own official URL or do not index it. Pretending that a filtered list and the full list are the same page is how a canonical becomes a lie.

Case and index files belong on the same list. `/About` and `/about` should not both be real. `/work/index.html` should not sit beside `/work`. These look like developer trivia until a shared link uses the ugly one and that ugly one starts to rank.

## How a small site gets cut into pieces

Imagine a studio with a homepage, a work index, eight project pages, and a dozen essays. That is a focused site. It can still fragment.

The homepage exists at the apex, at `/index.html`, and at a version with a slash the CDN added. The work index exists with and without the slash, and once with `?sort=year` left over from a prototype. Each essay exists on the production host and on a preview host that was left indexable. Each project page was shared from a staging link during review, and one of those links got copied into a partner's article.

None of these is a dramatic bug. Together they mean the essay you spent a week on is six URLs, each with a fraction of the links. [Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the site has a primary purpose, and whether a page is substantial next to other results. A primary purpose is hard to see when the same page introduces itself six times. The guidance also warns against producing lots of near-duplicate pages in the hope that some of them rank. Accidental duplicates are not a content mill, but they rhyme with one. The fix is the same: one page, one address, one reason to exist.

Hanabi builds this kind of marketing site in Next.js, on Vercel, with the repository in the client's hands. The framework will not save you from a vague host decision. It will faithfully emit whatever you configured, including two hosts if the domain records say so. The work is to choose, then to make redirects and metadata tell the same story.

## What to set before launch

Do this in the week the domain moves, not in a later cleanup. Cleanup is how preview URLs become permanent.

1. Choose the host and the slash rule, and write them in the launch notes.
2. Redirect every other host, protocol, and slash to that choice.
3. Emit a canonical on each page that matches the URL you actually serve after redirects.
4. Point the sitemap, the navigation, and the internal links at those same URLs.
5. Keep staging and preview deployments out of the index.

Then click the site the way a stranger will. Open the www version. Open a link with a trailing slash you do not use. Open a link with a leftover query. Each one should land on the official URL, once, without a chain of three redirects. Chains waste the first moment and sometimes drop the path.

Look at a project page you are proud of. Down the Cove, Thomas Bewick, and Ballarat Box Sports are public examples of work a studio might show. Whatever your set is, each project should have one URL you would send to the client. If the case study exists in a draft path and a launch path, pick the launch path and redirect the draft. Do not leave both "just in case the old one is bookmarked" without a redirect. Bookmarks survive. Ambiguity should not.

## When a canonical is the wrong tool

A canonical is not a redirect. If you control the duplicate, redirect it. Use the canonical for the copies you cannot fully collapse: tagged campaign links, a printer view you truly need, a parameter a third-party tool appends. If you can collapse it, do that. People and browsers follow redirects. Crawlers treat a canonical as advice.

Do not point a canonical at a page with different content to "concentrate" rankings. That is how a project page disappears behind the homepage, or an essay about pricing starts claiming to be an essay about process. The official URL should be a URL whose visible content matches. If the content has moved, redirect. If the content is gone, say so. A canonical that papers over a real change will confuse the next person who maintains the site, including you.

Do not set a different canonical in the CMS, the HTML, and the hosting headers. One source of truth. On a Next.js app, generate it from the same helper that builds internal links, so a change of host does not require a treasure hunt. Metadata scattered across a layout, a page file, and a proxy rule is how www comes back six months later.

Self-referencing canonicals are fine. A page that states its own official URL is being clear, not redundant. What is not fine is a template that points every page at the homepage because someone copied an example and left the href static. Check three page types before you ship: the homepage, a project, and an essay. If all three name the homepage, the template is wrong.

## A small audit you can repeat

Once a year, or after any domain change, export the URLs you know about and visit them. Include the sitemap, the last month of shared links, and a crawl of your own navigation. You are looking for twins: same title, different path. Merge them.

Also look at the title Google shows, when you have search results to look at. If the title in the result is not the title you wrote, read Google's list of common causes: a half-empty title, an obsolete date, boilerplate repeated across the set, or no single heading that is obviously the main one. Sometimes the title is the problem. Sometimes the URL is, and the title is only the symptom. Fix the address first, then judge the words.

The pages you keep should be ones you would send a founder. [Selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is the public set Hanabi puts forward: projects with a constraint, not a pile of near-duplicate case studies. That is the same instinct as a canonical. One page has to be the page.

After the address is stable, the picture people see when they paste it into a chat still has to match the article. [Open Graph images that match the article](/blog/open-graph-images-that-match-the-article) is the next piece, because a single official URL with a confusing preview still loses the introduction you meant to make.
